S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.

subtypes.With Depressed Mood: Symptoms mainly include low mood, tearfulness, or feelings of hopelessness.
subtypes.With Anxiety: Symptoms mainly include nervousness, worry, jitteriness, or separation anxiety.
subtypes.With Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood: A combination of depression and anxiety symptoms appears.
subtypes.With Disturbance of Conduct: Symptoms mainly involve violation of rules, truancy, vandalism, reckless driving, or fighting.
subtypes.With Mixed Disturbance of Emotions and C: Both emotional symptoms (depression, anxiety) and behavioral problems appear together.
subtypes.Unspecified: Maladaptive reactions not classified into the above types (e.g., physical complaints, social withdrawal).

symptom.disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral disturbances within three months of an identifiable psychosocial stressor, with distress out of proportion to the severity or intensity of the stressor and/or significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. The presentation is heterogeneous and can include anxious, depressed, or mixed emotional features, as well as maladaptive behavioral responses such as withdrawal, conflict, or decline in role performance. By definition, the disturbance does not represent normal bereavement, does not meet criteria for another mental disorder, and symptoms do not persist for more than six months after the stressor or its consequences have ended. It is often seen in the context of life transitions, interpersonal conflicts, health problems, or occupational stress, and is distinguished from more severe mood or anxiety disorders by its time-limited, stressor-linked course and relatively circumscribed impairment.

patient.personality: Paul is a quietly introspective, methodical historian who finds comfort in routine, solitary hobbies, and careful financial planning.
patient.stressor: Over the past year, Paul’s freelance work had been gradually shrinking as several regional journals cut budgets and the historical society he collaborated with shifted to in‑house staff, but he reassured himself he could make do by tightening expenses. The turning point came when his largest ongoing contract for digitizing a private Gettysburg collection was abruptly cancelled after the donor redirected funds, leaving him with a sudden and substantial drop in income and no clear replacement project. For someone who has long used meticulous budgeting, cataloging, and quiet, structured work as anchors after his divorce, the loss of this contract felt like a direct threat to both his financial stability and his identity as a valued historian, and over the following month he became increasingly preoccupied with the possibility of depleting his savings, stalling out professionally, and having to sell family heirlooms or his home. As these worries began to interfere with his ability to concentrate on smaller projects, maintain his usual volunteer archival work, and enjoy his solitary walks and gardening, a friend from the historical society urged him to see a psychiatrist, prompting him to seek help when he realized the stress around this setback was starting to disrupt his daily functioning.
patient.chief_complaint: “Ever since I lost my main contract, I feel like I’m not handling the stress in a normal way and it’s starting to affect how I function day to day.”

S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.
S081.manifestation: Since that contract fell through, I’ve been swinging between sitting at my desk staring at the same spreadsheet of dwindling savings for an hour, feeling this heavy, almost panicky dread about the future, and then snapping at friends who suggest I just ‘ride it out,’ and I’ve even been avoiding my usual volunteer shift at the archives because I can’t bear the thought of people asking how work is going.
